subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Into the Forest: Setting the Scene
periods.textbook_anchor: A Journey Through a Forest — Reena and Amit travel to their village near a forest for a harvest festival that coincides with the village becoming fully solar-powered (p. 57)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of the forest journey scene

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites children to share a time they travelled somewhere special — a village, a forest edge, a farm — and what they noticed around them. Two or three children share briefly; the teacher draws out sensory details (sounds, smells, colours).

Children open Textbook p. 57 and follow along as the teacher reads aloud the opening narrative of Reena and Amit's journey. The teacher pauses to ask: What do you think the village looks like? What might a harvest festival feel like?

Paired talk: each pair discusses two questions — What is a harvest festival? and What does it mean for a village to run entirely on sunlight? Pairs share one idea each; the teacher weaves responses into a brief class picture of the dual celebration.

The teacher closes by inviting children to think of one question they have about life in a village near a forest. Children whisper their question to a partner, then one or two are shared aloud. The teacher notes them on the board as 'things we want to find out'.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe a narrative setting by connecting personal experience to new contextual information.
periods.section_context: Reena and Amit's forest journey, harvest festival, solar-powered village, dual celebration framing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What do you think the village felt like the morning the lights came on for the first time?' This opens both the energy strand and the harvest-celebration strand without pre-answering either.

periods.activity_title: Flame of the Forest: Naming Local Flowers
periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — Write names of five colourful flowers in your area. For example, Palash is called Kesuda in Gujarat (p. 58)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of the Palash tree in bloom

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 58 and examine the Palash tree image. The teacher reads the description of its orange-red blooms and the name 'flame of forest', then asks: Does any plant or tree near our school or home have a special local name? A few children respond.

Children work individually to record in their notebooks the names of five colourful flowers from their own area — writing the common name and, if known, a local-language name alongside. They may also sketch a quick outline of one flower they know well.

A gallery share: children read their lists aloud one flower at a time while the teacher builds a class list on the board, grouping flowers by colour. The class notices which colours appear most often in their collective list.

The teacher closes with a brief reflection: plants have different names in different languages — the same flower may carry three or four names across India. Children write one new flower name they heard today that they did not know before.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record local natural features using multiple names and language contexts.
periods.section_context: Palash tree, 'flame of forest' name, Kesuda (Gujarat local name), five colourful flowers from children's own area.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt children who name flowers in their home language — write those names on the board with pride. Ask: 'Do you know if this flower is used for anything at home, in worship, or in cooking?' This surfaces the connection between plants and daily life naturally.

periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — Make the model of a house using materials from nature such as clay, wooden sticks, hay, grass, leaves, etc. Decorate it with an art form of your choice (p. 60)
materials: Rice flour paste or white paint (for wall decoration)
Newspaper or plastic sheet to protect desks
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of village house with clay walls and wall painting (p. 60)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 60 and look at the village house. The teacher describes how clay, hay, and cow dung are used in construction and how the grandmother paints walls with rice flour and water dye. Class briefly discusses: why might these materials have been chosen in the first place?

Children build a small model house using the natural materials on their desks — clay or mud forms the walls, sticks support corners, dry grass layers the roof. Once the structure is shaped, they add a simple wall decoration (dots, lines, flower shapes) using rice flour paste or white paint, inspired by the traditional painting shown in the textbook.

A quick gallery walk: children move around tables to look at each other's houses. They leave a 'comment stone' — a small pebble placed next to a house they found interesting — then return to their seats and share what caught their eye.
The teacher closes by asking: which part of your house came entirely from something natural? Children name one material and where it would come from in a real village.

periods.implied_lo: Students can construct a simple model using natural materials and explain the connection between local materials and built structures.
periods.section_context: Clay, hay, cow dung, wooden sticks, wall paintings with rice flour and water dye, traditional village house construction.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Your grandmother or someone older in your family — do they remember houses built this way, or do they still use any of these materials at home?' This invites traditional knowledge into the making activity without making it a separate task.

periods.activity_title: Colours from Plants: Making a Natural Dye
periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — Prepare a natural dye by boiling collected plant parts, straining the liquid, and painting a piece of cloth with the dye (p. 60)
materials: Petals of brightly coloured flowers (hibiscus, marigold, or locally available)
Heat source (school lab burner or induction plate)
Small pieces of light-coloured cloth or old handkerchief
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image or description of natural dye-making process (p. 60)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 60 and read the dye-making steps together. The teacher asks: before we had synthetic dyes, where do you think all the colours in fabric and art came from? Two or three children respond, then the teacher connects to the plant materials on the desks.

Working in small groups, children follow the textbook steps: place flower petals or beetroot in water, heat until the water changes colour, then strain the liquid into a cup. Each group then dips a small piece of cloth into their dye and observes how the colour transfers. Children note in their notebooks: which plant, what colour the water became, what the cloth looks like after dyeing.

Groups compare results across the class: whose dye was darkest? Which plant gave the most vivid colour? The teacher records the class's observations on the board in a simple two-column layout (plant material — colour result).

Children write one sentence in their notebooks completing: 'The colour we got came from ___ because ___.' The teacher closes by noting that the same process has been used by communities across India for generations to colour cloth and decorate homes.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a step-by-step investigation, observe an outcome, and record results in an organised way.
periods.section_context: Natural dyes from plant extracts, flowers, leaves, beetroot, hibiscus, marigold, boiling and straining method, painting cloth with plant-based dye.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do you know if anyone in your family uses natural colours for any purpose — for Holi, for rangoli, for cooking, for fabric?' This draws out cultural knowledge of plant-based colour use without interrupting the investigation.

periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — Find out some traditional ways of preserving grains and vegetables at your place and fill the table (p. 62)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of earthen grain-storage pot and bamboo basket (p. 62)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 62 and examine the images of earthen storage pots lined with neem leaves and bamboo baskets coated with cow dung. The teacher explains what each method does — neem and cow dung both repel insects — and asks: have you seen any of these at home or at a relative's house?

Small-group discussion: each group pools what its members know about traditional methods used in their homes or communities to preserve grains, pulses, or vegetables — not just the method, but also why it works. Groups fill the textbook table together, aiming for at least two or three methods per group.

Whole-class share: one person from each group reports a method; the teacher writes each on the board. The class looks for patterns — which methods use plants? Which use containers? Which use temperature or dryness?

Brief reflection: children write in their notebooks one method they had not heard of before today and one question they would like to ask an elder about it. The teacher notes that many of these methods have been passed down without being written down anywhere.

periods.implied_lo: Students can gather and organise information about traditional practices from community knowledge and describe how those practices serve a practical purpose.
periods.section_context: Earthen pots lined with neem leaves, bamboo baskets coated with cow dung, traditional grain and vegetable preservation methods, neem and cow dung as insect repellents.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think people chose neem leaves specifically, and not some other leaf?' This invites reasoning about plant properties and surfaces knowledge of neem from children's own experience without pre-answering.

periods.activity_title: Plants as Medicine: First Aid from Nature
periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — Discuss with the elders in your family and write the name of the plant, its parts, and its uses in the table given below (p. 63)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook table of medicinal plants and their uses (p. 63)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a scenario: imagine you are in the village and a child scrapes their knee — there is no pharmacy nearby. What would you do? Children brainstorm aloud. The teacher then opens Textbook p. 63 and the class looks at the medicinal plant table together.

Children fill in the table individually with plant names, parts used, and uses that they know from home or community experience. They may draw on what family elders have shown or told them. The teacher circulates, asking quiet follow-up questions to draw out additional knowledge.

Whole-class share: the teacher builds a collective list on the board. The class then addresses the two discussion prompts from the textbook — What should a first-aid box contain? and Why is giving first aid important? — using both the plant knowledge gathered and any other items children name.

Children write two sentences: one naming a plant remedy from their family tradition and what it is used for, and one sentence explaining why quick first aid matters. The teacher closes by affirming that knowing these plant uses is a form of practical knowledge many families carry.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe the practical uses of familiar plants based on community knowledge and apply that knowledge to a safety context.
periods.section_context: Medicinal plants, plant parts and their uses, first-aid box contents, importance of first aid for injuries, neem oil as natural mosquito repellent.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there a plant your family always keeps at home for health reasons — maybe in the kitchen or in a pot outside?' This opens up turmeric, tulsi, aloe, and other commonly known plants without leading children to a single answer.

periods.activity_title: Honey, Songs, and the Jenu Kurubas
periods.textbook_anchor: Welcome to the Village! — The Jenu Kurubas tribe of Karnataka sings apology songs to bees when harvesting honey, illustrating Indigenous respect for nature (p. 62)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook text or image relating to the Jenu Kurubas honey-harvesting tradition

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the passage about the Jenu Kurubas of Karnataka — a community that sings an apology song to bees before harvesting honey. Children listen, then share their initial reaction: does this practice surprise you? Why might someone apologise to bees?

Small-group discussion: What does this apology song tell us about how the Jenu Kurubas think about nature? Do children know of any practice in their own community where people show respect or gratitude to animals, plants, or the environment before using them? Groups share one example each.

Whole-class reflection: the teacher draws out the idea that taking from nature with care — taking only what is needed, showing gratitude, leaving the rest — is a value different communities hold in different ways. Children identify one value they see in the Jenu Kurubas practice (care, gratitude, restraint, respect).

Children write a short response: 'If I were going to take something from nature, I would show respect by ___.' Two or three children read aloud. The teacher closes by noting that this attitude is one many communities around India share, each in their own way.

periods.implied_lo: Students can examine a cultural practice, identify the value it expresses, and connect that value to their own experience of respecting living things.
periods.section_context: Jenu Kurubas tribe of Karnataka, apology songs to bees before honey harvest, respect for nature, traditional ecological values.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you think of any time your family or community does something special before cutting a tree, harvesting crops, or taking water from a well?' This surfaces local practices of gratitude and restraint without requiring any particular answer.

periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — Talk to your elders and find out the rituals in connection to animals and plants which are celebrated in your locality (p. 66)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images or descriptions of Vat Purnima, Hari Jiroti, and Kaziranga Elephant Festival (p. 66)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 66 and the teacher introduces the three nature-connected festivals described — Vat Purnima (Banyan tree), Hari Jiroti (fruit-bearing trees), and the Kaziranga Elephant Festival. The teacher asks: have you heard of any festival where a tree, animal, or plant is at the centre of the celebration?

Children fill the textbook table individually or in pairs: they write the name of a local ritual or festival connected to a plant or animal that they know from their own family or community, when it is held, and what happens during it. The teacher circulates and encourages children who are unsure to think of Pongal, Onam, Nag Panchami, or any seasonal practice they have witnessed.

Whole-class share: the class builds a collective map on the board — festival name, plant or animal connection, and region or community. The teacher draws attention to the variety: the same tree (Banyan) may be celebrated in multiple ways in different places.

Children write one sentence explaining what they think connects all these festivals: what do they all seem to say about the relationship between people and nature? Two or three responses are read aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe connections between cultural celebrations and the natural world by drawing on personal and community experience.
periods.section_context: Vat Purnima (Banyan tree worship), Hari Jiroti (fruit-bearing trees), Kaziranga Elephant Festival, harvest festival, nature-worship traditions across India.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there a tree, animal, or plant that your family treats with special care — one that you would never cut or harm?' This draws out Sacred Grove thinking and local reverence for nature before the class encounters the formal term.

periods.activity_title: Sacred Groves and the Village Lit by Sun
periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — Imagine if there is no electricity in your area for two days. What changes will you see in your life? (p. 65)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook description of the solar-powered village celebration and Sacred Groves passage

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening of Textbook p. 65 — the village lit up by solar power for the harvest festival, people in traditional dress, dhol and nagada drums. Children close their eyes and picture the scene. The teacher then poses the discussion question from the textbook: imagine no electricity for two days — what changes?

Children list in their notebooks all the things at home or school that need electricity, then circle the ones they consider most important for daily life and safety. Pairs compare lists and mark items that appear on both.

The teacher introduces Sacred Groves from the same section — small forest patches that communities protect for worship and wildlife. Children read the relevant passage. Discussion: how is protecting a Sacred Grove similar to what the Jenu Kurubas did when they sang to bees before harvesting honey? What idea connects both?

Children write two observations in their notebooks: one about what solar energy makes possible in a village, and one about what a Sacred Grove protects. The teacher closes by noting that both solar energy and Sacred Groves reflect communities finding ways to live with nature rather than against it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe how communities use natural resources sustainably and describe the relationship between energy, light, and daily life.
periods.section_context: Solar-powered village, harvest festival celebration, electricity dependence, Sacred Groves as community-protected forest patches, dhol and nagada drums, traditional dress and prayers.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do you know of any place in your area — a grove, a pond, a hill — that people treat as sacred and do not disturb?' This surfaces local Sacred Grove equivalents and helps children see the concept as alive, not just historical.

periods.activity_title: What We Take, What We Owe: Reflecting on Natural Resources
periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — What are the things that we use from nature in our daily life? What challenges arise when we overuse natural resources? (p. 67)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 67 and read the first two reflection prompts silently: What do we use from nature daily? and What happens when we overuse resources? The teacher gives an example for wood (forests deplete) and then asks children to think about water, soil, and sea products.

Children work individually to write their responses in their notebooks: first a list of things they personally use from nature every day (food, water, wood, cloth fibres, air), then for each overuse challenge prompt — water, soil, sea products — one sentence about what depletion might look like in their own experience or community.

Pairs share their lists. The class builds a collective 'we use from nature' list on the board, then maps one consequence against each resource. The teacher guides the class to notice that some consequences are already visible in their own locality.

Children write one reflective sentence completing: 'The natural resource I think I use most without thinking is ___, and one thing I could do differently is ___.' Two or three children share aloud. The teacher affirms that noticing is the first step toward acting.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify natural resources used in daily life and describe the consequences of overusing a specific resource.
periods.section_context: Natural resources used daily (water, wood, soil, food, cloth), consequences of overusing water, soil, sea products, wood; forests depleting; nature's contribution to eating, clothing, and healthcare.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has your family ever noticed a change — a river getting smaller, a type of fish disappearing, a tree that used to be common that you rarely see now?' This grounds abstract resource depletion in children's lived observation.

periods.activity_title: My Herbal Garden: Drawing Our Connection to Nature
periods.textbook_anchor: Sparkling Light, Happy Life — Design your herbal garden. Draw pictures of your favorite herbs in different parts of the garden and write down their names (p. 68)
materials: Drawing paper or open notebook page
periods.visual_aids: Textbook herbal garden design prompt and example layout (p. 68)

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 68 and read the herbal garden design prompt. The teacher asks: which herbs or useful plants do you already know by name? Children call out names (tulsi, mint, aloe, turmeric, curry leaf, neem) and the teacher lists them on the board as a reference bank.

Children design their herbal garden on drawing paper: they divide the space into sections, draw each herb in its part of the garden, write its name, and add a brief label of what it is good for. The textbook prompt also asks them to include herbs they like less — children are encouraged to include at least one unfamiliar or disliked plant and write why they included it anyway.

A gallery share: children prop their garden drawings on the desk and do an unhurried walk around the class, pausing at gardens that have an herb they have not drawn. They return to their seats and add one new herb to their own garden if they found one they want to include.

Children write one sentence: 'My garden shows that nature gives us ___.' Two or three are read aloud. The teacher closes by noting that even a small herbal garden is one way of keeping a connection to plants alive in daily life.

periods.implied_lo: Students can communicate their understanding of plant uses through a designed visual product that connects personal knowledge to a broader relationship with nature.
periods.section_context: Herbal garden design, favourite herbs, herb names and uses, conservation through planting, reducing paper waste, avoiding plastic, feeding birds, clean-up drives.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there a plant in your garden that you were told never to cut or remove? Why do you think that instruction was given?' This invites children to connect the conservation actions in this section to values they already hold.

assessment_items.question_text: Reena and Amit's village was celebrating two things at the same time. Which of the following best describes what made this celebration special?

options.label: A
options.text: The village won an award for the best harvest in the district.

options.label: B
options.text: The harvest festival happened on the same day the village began running fully on solar energy.

options.label: C
options.text: A new school was opened in the village on the day of the harvest festival.

options.label: D
options.text: Reena and Amit visited the village for the first time during a forest festival.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This tests recall of the chapter's framing narrative and the dual celebration that opens the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe a narrative setting by connecting personal experience to new contextual information.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the child read a general idea of celebration but missed the solar-energy milestone — they retained 'harvest' but not the clean-energy strand.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates a guess or confusion; a school opening is not mentioned in the chapter and reveals the child did not engage with the narrative.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the setting — Reena and Amit do travel to the village and there is a forest, but the festival is a harvest celebration, not a forest festival, and it is not their first visit.

assessment_items.question_text: The Palash tree is called the 'flame of the forest'. In Gujarat, it is known as Kesuda. Why do you think the same tree might have different names in different places? Give one reason and write one example of a flower from your area with its local name.
expected_elements: A reason why the same plant may have different names in different places (e.g., different languages, different communities, different regions use different words).
One flower name from the child's own area.
A local or regional name for that flower (in any language the child knows).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any plausible local flower and any local-language name. Regional variation is inherent — a child naming any flower with any local name is correct. Award full credit for any thoughtful reason about language or regional variation, even if simply stated. This item carries a regional-variation note: any locally known flower and its local name is an acceptable and correct answer.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record local natural features using multiple names and language contexts.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: A reason why the same plant may have different names in different places (e.g., different languages, different communities, different regions use different words).
One flower name from the child's own area.
A local or regional name for that flower (in any language the child knows).

assessment_items.task: You are going to build a tiny model house the way village houses are made — using only natural materials. Use clay or mud for the walls, sticks or twigs for the frame, and dry grass or leaves for the roof. When your house is ready, add one wall decoration in the style of traditional wall paintings (dots, lines, or flower shapes using white paste or light colour). Be ready to say: which part of your house came from a plant, and which came from the earth?
assessment_items.scaffold: 1. Shape your walls using clay or mud. 2. Add a stick or twig frame. 3. Layer dry grass or leaves on top for the roof. 4. Paint or draw one simple pattern on the wall. 5. Write (or say): one material from a plant — ___ ; one material from the earth — ___.
format_of_output: Small 3D model house made from natural materials
At least one wall decoration applied to the model
One spoken or written sentence identifying a plant-based material and an earth-based material used
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the model on whether natural materials were used (not whether it looks polished) and whether the child can name one plant-sourced and one earth-sourced component. Any natural material available locally is acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a simple model using natural materials and explain the connection between local materials and built structures.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can translate knowledge of natural building materials into a tangible artefact and articulate why those materials were chosen.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The five steps guide children through building then labelling — the labelling step is where understanding of material origin is demonstrated. A child who builds without completing step 5 has only partially met the task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: model uses at least two different natural materials; wall decoration is present; child can name and distinguish a plant-based from an earth-based material. Weak: model made from non-natural materials (paper, plastic); no decoration; child cannot name the origin of any material.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who cannot shape clay may draw a detailed diagram of the house with labels for each material. Children with motor difficulties may describe their design verbally while a partner builds.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: 3D model with oral or written labelling
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The task mirrors the textbook activity exactly and allows children to demonstrate material knowledge through making, not just describing.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wants to make a natural dye from beetroot. She fills a pot with water, drops in beetroot pieces, and immediately strains out the beetroot without heating the water. She finds the dye is very pale. What did she miss doing, and why does it matter?
expected_elements: Identification of the missing step: heating or boiling the water with the plant material.
An explanation of why heating matters: it draws the colour out of the plant material into the water.
A link to the observed result: without heating, little colour is released, so the dye is weak or pale.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any equivalent explanation of the heating step. The child does not need to use the word 'extract' — any everyday phrasing (the colour stays inside the beetroot, the water does not get the colour) is acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a step-by-step investigation, observe an outcome, and record results in an organised way.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: Identification of the missing step: heating or boiling the water with the plant material.
An explanation of why heating matters: it draws the colour out of the plant material into the water.
A link to the observed result: without heating, little colour is released, so the dye is weak or pale.

assessment_items.question_text: In a village, grain is stored in earthen pots lined with neem leaves and in bamboo baskets coated with cow dung. What is the main reason for using these materials?

options.label: A
options.text: Neem leaves and cow dung make the containers smell pleasant.

options.label: B
options.text: Neem leaves and cow dung help keep insects away from the stored grain.

options.label: C
options.text: Neem leaves keep the grain warm, and cow dung keeps it cold.

options.label: D
options.text: These materials are used because they are cheaper than plastic containers.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This tests understanding of the practical function of traditional grain-storage methods as described in the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can gather and organise information about traditional practices from community knowledge and describe how those practices serve a practical purpose.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the child associated the materials with sensory properties rather than their functional, insect-repelling role — a surface-level engagement with the content.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the child guessed based on a general idea that different substances affect temperature, without recalling the insect-repellent function described in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a cost-comparison idea not present in the chapter — indicates the child did not engage with the specific cultural-ecological reasoning and applied everyday consumer logic instead.

assessment_items.question_text: In the chapter, children are asked to discuss with family elders about plants and their uses. Imagine you spoke to an elder in your family and they told you about a plant used for a health purpose at home. Write about: (a) what plant they mentioned and what part is used, (b) what health problem it helps with, and (c) why you think knowing about this plant is useful for everyday life.
look_for: A specific plant named with the part used (leaf, root, bark, fruit, etc.).
A clear health use or purpose connected to that plant part.
A reasoned statement about why this knowledge is practically useful — not just that it is 'good to know' but how it helps in everyday situations.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any plant from any cultural or regional tradition. Answers will vary by family and region — all are valid. A child who names tulsi leaves for fever, or aloe gel for burns, or turmeric for cuts is equally correct to one who names a less-common plant. This item carries a regional-variation note: any locally known medicinal plant and use is an acceptable and correct answer.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe the practical uses of familiar plants based on community knowledge and apply that knowledge to a safety context.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

look_for: A specific plant named with the part used (leaf, root, bark, fruit, etc.).
A clear health use or purpose connected to that plant part.

A reasoned statement about why this knowledge is practically useful — not just that it is 'good to know' but how it helps in everyday situations (e.g., useful when a pharmacy is far away, useful for minor injuries at home, useful because the plant is easy to grow nearby).

assessment_items.task: Think about the Jenu Kurubas of Karnataka, who sing an apology song to bees before collecting honey. They take only what they need and show respect to the bees. Now think of one living thing — a plant, an animal, an insect, or a tree — that you or your community uses or depends on. Write a short message (3–5 sentences) to that living thing: say what you take from it, say thank you, and promise one way you will take care of it. You may also draw the living thing if you wish.
assessment_items.scaffold: 1. Name the living thing you are writing to. 2. Write what you or your community takes from it. 3. Write a thank-you sentence. 4. Write one promise: something you will do to care for or protect it. 5. (Optional) Draw the living thing.
format_of_output: Written message of 3–5 sentences addressed to a living thing
Optional: a drawing of the chosen living thing
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any living thing the child chooses — a cow, a tree, a river fish, a bee, a mango tree, tulsi, rice plant. The quality of the response lies in the reasoning (what is taken, a genuine thank-you, a specific promise) not in the choice of subject. This item carries a regional-variation note: any living thing significant to the child's own community is an acceptable choice.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can examine a cultural practice, identify the value it expresses, and connect that value to their own experience of respecting living things.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can transfer the value embedded in a cultural practice (respectful, limited taking from nature) to their own relationship with a living thing, moving from description to personal commitment.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Steps 1–2 establish the relationship; step 3 demonstrates gratitude; step 4 is the key evaluative step — a specific, actionable promise shows the child has internalised the value, not just described it.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific living thing; clear description of what is taken from it; a genuine and specific promise (not vague like 'I will be kind to nature'). Weak: vague or generic living thing (just 'nature'); no description of what is taken; promise is empty ('I will take care of it') without any specific action.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find writing difficult may draw the living thing first and then dictate or write single-word labels. Children may write in any language they are comfortable in.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Short written message with optional drawing
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The message format mirrors the spirit of the apology song — it is an act of communication directed at a living thing — making the task structurally connected to the cultural practice being assessed.

assessment_items.question_text: Vat Purnima, Hari Jiroti, and the Kaziranga Elephant Festival are all examples of something found across many parts of India. What do all three have in common?

options.label: A
options.text: They are all celebrated on the same day every year across India.

options.label: B
options.text: They all involve people worshipping or celebrating a specific animal or plant.

options.label: C
options.text: They are all harvest festivals that mark the end of the farming season.

options.label: D
options.text: They are all celebrated only in Karnataka and Gujarat.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This tests the child's ability to identify the common cultural-ecological thread across three distinct festivals described in the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe connections between cultural celebrations and the natural world by drawing on personal and community experience.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the child assumed a common calendar date — a guess not supported by the chapter; shows they did not engage with the distinct regional identities of the three festivals.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses these festivals with a harvest festival (which is separately described in the chapter) — the child may have blurred the different types of nature celebration described in the section.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Limits the festivals to two states mentioned in the chapter (Karnataka for Jenu Kurubas, Gujarat for Kesuda) — shows partial regional recall but misapplies it, missing that these three festivals are from different parts of India.

assessment_items.question_text: A village has a small patch of forest that no one cuts trees from or hunts in. The villagers say it belongs to the gods and must be kept untouched. What is this kind of protected forest called, and give one reason why protecting it is good for the village and for wildlife.
expected_elements: The term 'Sacred Grove' (or an equivalent description — a community-protected forest patch).
One reason the protection benefits the village (e.g., preserves water sources, provides forest resources sustainably, keeps the forest healthy).
One reason the protection benefits wildlife (e.g., animals have a safe undisturbed habitat, biodiversity is preserved).
assessment_items.annotation: If a child does not use the term 'Sacred Grove' but describes it accurately (a forest patch kept protected by the community for religious reasons), award full credit for the concept. The benefit reasons need not be technical — simple, clear reasoning is sufficient.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe how communities use natural resources sustainably and describe the relationship between energy, light, and daily life.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

expected_elements: The term 'Sacred Grove' or an accurate description of a community-protected forest patch.
One reason the protection benefits the village (e.g., forest remains a resource, water is preserved, the community has a healthy environment).
One reason the protection benefits wildlife (e.g., animals have an undisturbed habitat, many species can survive there safely).

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter says that if we overuse wood from forests, the forests deplete. Think about water as a natural resource. What happens when water is overused or wasted? Give two examples of the problems it causes, and suggest two things a family can do at home to use water more carefully.
look_for: Two distinct problems caused by overusing or wasting water (e.g., water sources dry up, animals and plants suffer, farming becomes difficult, drinking water becomes scarce).
Two specific, practical actions a family can take at home to reduce water waste (e.g., turning off taps when not in use, collecting rainwater, fixing leaky pipes, reusing washing water for plants).
A sense that the child understands the connection between individual action and the larger resource — that what a family does at home actually matters for the shared resource.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two plausible problems and any two practical home actions. Regional water contexts vary — a child in a drought-prone area may give different examples than one in a water-rich region; both are valid. This item carries a regional-variation note: problems and actions grounded in the child's local water context are acceptable and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify natural resources used in daily life and describe the consequences of overusing a specific resource.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

look_for: Two distinct, plausible consequences of water overuse (e.g., rivers and wells dry up; crops fail; animals cannot find water; drinking water becomes scarce; soil loses moisture).
Two specific and practical family-level actions to reduce water waste (e.g., turning off taps, using a bucket instead of a running hose, collecting rainwater, reusing water from washing vegetables).
Evidence that the child connects personal/family behaviour to the shared resource — not just listing actions but showing awareness that these actions protect a resource everyone depends on.

assessment_items.task: Design your own herbal garden on a full page. Divide the page into at least four sections. In each section, draw one herb or useful plant and write its name. Below each drawing, write one use of that plant — for example, for health, for cooking, for keeping insects away, or for any other purpose you know. Try to include at least one plant you are less familiar with.
assessment_items.scaffold: 1. Draw a simple garden outline on your page (four or more sections). 2. In each section, draw one herb or useful plant. 3. Write the plant's name clearly. 4. Write one use of that plant under its name. 5. Mark one plant with a star — the one you think is most important and write one sentence saying why.
format_of_output: A drawn garden layout with at least four sections on a full page
Each section contains a drawing of a plant with its name labelled
Each plant has one use written below it
One plant is starred with a sentence explaining why the child considers it most important
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any herbs or useful plants the child knows — from their home garden, kitchen, local area, or the chapter. There is no required plant list. The quality of the response lies in the specificity of the use written and the reasoning for the starred plant. This item carries a regional-variation note: any locally known herb or plant is an acceptable and correct choice.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can communicate their understanding of plant uses through a designed visual product that connects personal knowledge to a broader relationship with nature.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can organise knowledge of multiple plants into a designed layout and articulate specific uses, demonstrating that they understand plants as practical natural resources — not just as pictures in a book.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Steps 1–4 build the garden; step 5 is the evaluative step — the starred plant and the reason given reveals the depth of the child's connection to the material. A child who writes 'because it is pretty' has not demonstrated understanding of use; one who writes 'because it helps when someone has a cough and we always keep it at home' has.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: four or more distinct plants; uses are specific and accurate (e.g., 'for fever' rather than 'for health'); the starred plant reason explains a real connection to daily life or community need. Weak: fewer than four plants; uses are vague ('it is good for you'); the starred plant reason is arbitrary or absent.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find drawing difficult may write the plant name inside the section and label the parts with words. Children may name plants in any language they know — a local-language name is fully acceptable alongside or instead of an English name.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Labelled garden diagram with written uses
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The visual-plus-writing format matches the textbook task exactly and allows children to demonstrate both knowledge of plants and ability to organise information spatially.
